questions.question: 8.3% of this IPO's money is an offer for sale. Where does that part of the money go?

choices.text: Into the company, to build new factories.
To the existing owners who are selling their shares.

questions.explanation: In an offer for sale, existing owners sell shares they already hold, so the money goes to them. Only the fresh issue, ₹49.50 crore here, reaches A J Packaging Limited.

numbers.name: ofs_share
numbers.label: Share of the IPO money going to sellers

questions.question: Sales went from ₹210.03 crore in FY24 to ₹223.03 crore in FY26, which is 3% a year. How would you describe that?
questions.explanation: 3% a year is barely growing, or shrinking: A J Packaging Limited isn't selling much more than before.

questions.question: A J Packaging Limited owes 1.55 rupees of loans for every rupee of its owners' money. Which is closest to the truth?

choices.text: Its loans are small to manageable next to what the owners have put in.
Its loans are heavy: lenders have more riding on it than its owners.
Loans never matter for a company that makes a profit.

questions.explanation: At 1.55 rupees of loans per rupee of owners' money, lenders have more riding on A J Packaging Limited than its owners, and repayments are due even in bad years.

numbers.label: Loans for every rupee of owners' money

questions.question: An unofficial grey market premium of ₹24 a share is being quoted. How much should you rely on it?

choices.text: Completely: it tells you the listing price.
A little at most: it is unregulated and easy to push around.
It is set by the stock exchange.

questions.explanation: The grey market premium of ₹24 for A J Packaging Limited is gossip with a number on it: nobody regulates it, and it often turns out wrong.
